stories.title: Implement STUN NAT type probing in scp-transport
stories.description: Implement STUN binding requests (RFC 8489) in scp-transport to determine NAT type and external address on startup. NAT type classification (full-cone, address-restricted, port-restricted, symmetric) drives reachability tier selection (§10.12.1). STUN probing is performed against known SCP relays that serve as STUN endpoints. The result determines whether hole punching (Tier 2) is viable or bridge fallback (Tier 3) is required. 25-second keepalive maintains NAT mapping for non-symmetric NATs.

stories.title: Support ws:// transport for DHT-discovered relays
stories.description: Extend the relay WebSocket transport to accept ws:// (plaintext) connections for relay URLs from a resolved service record (§10.12.6). This enables self-hosted relays behind NAT with no domain to be reachable without requiring TLS certificates.

stories.title: Implement .no_domain() ApplicationNode builder mode

stories.title: Implement BRIDGE relay operation for symmetric NAT fallback
stories.description: Implement the BRIDGE operation (§10.12.4) as Tier 3 fallback for symmetric NAT (~15% of home routers). stories.title: Implement did_routing_id derivation function
stories.description: Implement the did_routing_id derivation (§3.10.2): SHA-256("scp:did:" || did_string). The "scp:did:" domain separator prevents collision with context routing IDs (HMAC-SHA256(identity_key, context_id) per §5.7.1) and broadcast routing IDs (SHA-256(context_id) per §5.14). This is a pure function with no dependencies — the building block for relay-based identity resolution.

stories.title: Implement key-event record PUBLISH to SCP relays via RepublishManager
stories.description: Extend RepublishManager to publish key-event records to SCP relays over the PUBLISH operation (§3.10.5). stories.title: Implement IdentityBackend::resolve with parallel multi-relay resolution
stories.description: Implement the IdentityBackend trait (§3.10.10), the protocol's one resolution entry point. resolve takes the identifier's 32 raw digest bytes and returns a ResolutionOutcome carrying a verdict, key state, and sources. The resolver queries the identity's own relays and the fallback set in parallel, with per-relay 10-second timeouts, and counts a response only where it verified that chain. Fork precedence ranks two diverging chains (§9.7.4.2 R6). The resolver settles and counts only the sources its page walk read to exhaustion (§3.10.4 steps 4 and 5).

ResolutionSources carries relays_reached, unexhausted, declared, proven, and head_provenance, with `declared` and `proven` holding 33-byte SEC1 compressed operator keys because R11's first-contact floor counts keys and never declared operator identifiers (`03-identity.md` §3.10.10, `09-security-model.md` §9.7.4.2 R11)
The resolver queries both relay sets concurrently via tokio::join! (§3.10.4 step 2)
The resolver decodes each response, recomputes its identifier from the inception event, and verifies every later event (§3.10.4)
A response failing any of those three checks is discarded

The resolver settles chains only from sources the page walk read to exhaustion, and a source it did not exhaust yields `Inconclusive{MissingEvents}`, except that a source holding two rank-1 suffixes may yield `Contested{Rank1Terminal}`: a test per case (§3.10.4 step 4, `09-security-model.md` §9.7.4.2 R9)

The first-contact floor counts a relay only where the walk read it to exhaustion, it served a chain that survived step 3, and its proof verified; `unexhausted` lists every relay the walk did not exhaust, and `proven` holds no key from such a relay: a test asserts all three (§3.10.4 step 5, §3.10.10)
A prefix chain loses to the longer chain (§3.10.4 step 4)

stories.title: Implement protocol-level healing of stale key-event records across resolution layers
stories.description: Per §3.10.7, when both resolution layers return valid documents with different sequence numbers, the resolver SHOULD re-publish the fresher document to the layer that returned the stale one (protocol-level healing). stories.title: Publish a bridge's routing target as the SCPRelay entry's bridgeTarget field
stories.description: A tier 3 bridge entry carried its routing target as a `?bridge_target=` query on the bridge relay's URL. §18.2.1 now gives the `SCPRelay` entry a `bridgeTarget` property: 64 lowercase hex digits naming the identity routing ID of §10.12.4.1, and the entry's `serviceEndpoint` is the bridge relay's own URL (§10.12.4 step 4, §10.12.7). §3.10.13 signs an `SCPRelay` entry's 32 trailing bytes as its `bridgeTarget`, and SHA-256(0x00) there means "no target", so a writer never names SHA-256(0x00) as a target. Every `SCPRelay` URL has a §9.18.2 canonical form whose path ends in /scp/v1, and a reader of the did:dht JSON document rejects an entry that fails §18.2.1 and keeps the record: a malformed, null or SHA-256(0x00) `bridgeTarget`, or a `bridgeTarget` on an entry whose type is not `SCPRelay`, rejects that entry only, and in every form a `bridgeTarget` on an entry whose URL is not `wss` rejects that entry only (§10.12.7). This story adds the validated `RelayEndpoint`, `BridgeEndpoint` and `BridgeTarget` types and `RelayService` to scp-did, so a relay entry a node publishes satisfies §18.2.1 by construction; moves the §9.18.2 canonicalizer from scp-protocol into scp-did so those constructors can call it; makes `DidDocument` drop every entry §18.2.1 rejects while it deserializes, so no reader sees one; makes the scp-node tier 3 publisher write the bridge relay's URL with `bridge_target`; and deletes the query-string bridge parser from scp-transport. The node publishes the routing ID that `verify_bridge_registration` checks today; the identifier-bytes value §10.12.4.1 defines arrives with SCP-315, the key-event-log identity cut-over. Sending `BRIDGE_REGISTER` from the node is not this story.

stories.title: Bridge relay opens per-peer sessions to a registered relay and carries their frames both ways under per-session caps
stories.description: Implements the bridge relay's half of the sessions that `10-infrastructure-and-self-hosting.md` §10.12.4 **Sessions** defines, and the frames and codes ADR-004 lists for them. Alec chose the option "Tunnel sessions" on 2026-10-20 (`00-open-questions.md`, entry "A response path from a bridged node to the peer"), in place of the reply path he had chosen earlier that day. Today the bridge forwards a peer's `BRIDGE_DATA` with a zeroed `source_routing_id` (`handle_bridge_data` in `crates/scp-transport/src/native/server.rs`) and keeps no record of the peer, so nothing the node sends can reach the peer. This story adds `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN`, `BRIDGE_SESSION_CREDIT` and `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE`, gives `BRIDGE_DATA` a `session_id` in both directions in place of `target_routing_id` and `source_routing_id`, adds the codes `4033` BRIDGE_SESSION_UNKNOWN and `4035` BRIDGE_FLOW_VIOLATION, and makes the bridge keep one record per session under the identifier, credit, cap, close and connection-loss rules of §10.12.4. The self-hosted relay's side and the peer's session call are SCP-340. SCP has no deployed users, so `BRIDGE_DATA` changes shape with no compatibility path. Function, type and field names in Rust are indicators; the wire field names are the spec's.
acceptanceCriteria: Wire types (§10.12.4 **Sessions**, ADR-004 frame tables): `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` carries `session_id: u64` and `target_routing_id: bin32` in both directions, and `source_tag: bin16` from the bridge to the registered connection; `BRIDGE_DATA` carries `session_id: u64` and `payload: bin` in both directions, with no `target_routing_id` and no `source_routing_id`; `BRIDGE_SESSION_CREDIT` carries `session_id: u64` and `bytes: u32`; `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` carries `session_id: u64` and `code: u16`; each carries the optional `ref`. MessagePack round-trip tests pin each field name and type in each direction, and `git grep -n -w -e source_routing_id -e forward_id -e BridgeReply -e BRIDGE_OPEN -e BRIDGE_CREDIT -e BRIDGE_CLOSE -e BridgeOpen -e BridgeCredit -e BridgeClose crates/` prints nothing.
Codes: `crates/scp-relay-client/src/error.rs` defines `4033` BRIDGE_SESSION_UNKNOWN and `4035` BRIDGE_FLOW_VIOLATION as client errors, and the constant-value test asserts both.

Opening (§10.12.4 **Opening**, **Session identifiers**): a peer's `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` for a registered target reaches the registered connection as a `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` with the same `target_routing_id` and a session ID the bridge chose, and the peer gets `OK` echoing its `ref`; a test opens 1,000 sessions from ten peers to one registered connection and finds the registered connection's session IDs strictly increasing, and the bridge's session table maps each to its peer connection and peer session ID. Each refusal opens nothing on the registered connection: `4030` with brokering disabled, `4032` for an unregistered target, `4003` for a `session_id` equal to and one lower than an ID the peer already used on that connection, and `4031` beyond a session cap. Sessions opened from one source address over two connections carry one `source_tag` on the registered connection, and so do sessions from two IPv6 addresses in one /64; sessions from two IPv4 addresses, or from two IPv6 /64s, carry different tags; with `ipv6_source_prefix` set to 56, two /64s in one /56 carry one tag; and the same prefix's sessions on two registered connections carry different tags. A test vector fixes `tag_key`, an IPv4 address and an IPv6 address and checks each `source_tag` against `HMAC-SHA256(tag_key, family || prefix_len || prefix)` truncated to 16 bytes. A `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` sent on a registered connection gets `ERR` `4000`.

IPv4-mapped sources (§10.12.4 **Caps**, ADR-004 `ipv6_source_prefix`): on a bridge listening on a dual-stack socket, two IPv4 peers, which the socket reports as `::ffff:a.b.c.d` and `::ffff:w.x.y.z`, get different `source_tag`s on the registered connection and separate per-prefix session caps and rate buckets: with the per-prefix session cap lowered to 1, each opens one session and neither gets `4031`. The `source_tag` of an IPv4 peer is the same whether it arrives on the dual-stack socket or on an IPv4-only socket, matching the `family` 4 test vector of the opening criterion.

Data and order (§10.12.4 **Data**): with two peers that each hold two sessions to one registered connection, `BRIDGE_DATA` frames sent in interleaved order in both directions reach the other end of their own session only, in the order sent, with the payload byte-for-byte equal and the other leg's session ID. A payload that is not MessagePack is carried unchanged, which shows the bridge does not decode it. The bridge writes no frame in answer to a `BRIDGE_DATA`, `BRIDGE_SESSION_CREDIT` or `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` it accepts. A `BRIDGE_DATA` whose payload exceeds `max_blob_size` plus 1,024 bytes closes the session with `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` `4010` on both legs and none of its bytes reach the other end.

Backpressure (§10.12.4 **Backpressure**): a session opens with zero credit in each direction, and after opening the bridge sends the peer and the registered connection each a `BRIDGE_SESSION_CREDIT` no larger than its per-session buffer and drawn from the token buckets of the next criterion. A `BRIDGE_DATA` within its sender's credit is carried; one beyond it closes the session with `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` `4035` on both legs and none of its bytes reach the other end. A test in which the receiving end grants no credit shows the bridge holds no more buffered payload for that session and direction than the credit it granted the sender, forwards nothing to the receiving end, and keeps carrying the frames of another session on the same registered connection.

Caps as configuration (§10.12.4 **Caps**, ADR-052, `.docs/standards/construction.md`): the bridge's relay configuration carries sessions per source prefix, sessions per registered connection, payload bytes per second per session direction, payload bytes per second per source prefix direction, the per-session buffer and `ipv6_source_prefix` as named fields of its flat config object, defaulting to 8, 256, 1 MiB, 2 MiB, `max_blob_size` plus 1,024 bytes and 64; no global, singleton or `static` holds them, and `scripts/check-no-mutable-globals.sh` passes. Tests with the caps lowered show: a `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` beyond the per-source-prefix cap gets `4031` and opens nothing when one address spreads its sessions over several connections, and when several IPv6 addresses in one /64 each open sessions; an open from another IPv4 address or another /64 still succeeds; a `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` beyond the per-registered-connection cap gets `4031`. Under a paused Tokio clock: a sender that has used its session bucket's tokens receives no further `BRIDGE_SESSION_CREDIT` until the clock advances, and the session stays open; two sessions of one source prefix, from two IPv6 addresses in one /64, together receive no more credit per second than the per-prefix rate plus one bucket; a session left idle for an hour then receives at most `max_blob_size` plus 1,024 bytes of credit before the bucket refills, which shows no burst accrues. No per-connection rate limit applies to session frames, and the bridge reads no payload byte to enforce a cap.

Closing (§10.12.4 **Closing**): a `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` from either end frees the session and reaches the other end exactly once, with the same code and that leg's session ID; a `BRIDGE_DATA` for that session that crossed the close is dropped and answered with nothing; a `BRIDGE_DATA`, `BRIDGE_SESSION_CREDIT` or `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` naming a session ID greater than every ID opened on its connection gets `ERR` `4033` and reaches no connection. A test counts the frames written to every connection before and after each case.

Connection loss (§10.12.4 **Connection loss**): when a peer connection closes, every session it held is freed and the registered connection receives `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` with code `0` for each, carrying each session's registered-leg ID; when a registered connection closes, each of its sessions' peers receives `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` `4032` with its own session ID, and a later `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` for its routing ID gets `4032` (§10.12.4 **Bridge establishment** step 5). A test asserts the session table is empty after both.
actionItems: Add the session frames and change `BridgeData` in `scp-relay-client`.
Add the session table beside `BridgeRegistry`, keyed by connection and session ID, with credit and a buffer per direction and a per-connection index for connection loss.
Handle the session frames in the native relay server and add the cap fields to the relay configuration.

stories.title: A bridged self-hosted relay serves each bridge session as a listener connection, and a peer opens sessions through a bridge
stories.description: Implements the self-hosted relay's side and the peer's side of `10-infrastructure-and-self-hosting.md` §10.12.4 **Sessions**, over the frames and bridge sessions of SCP-339. Today the native relay client discards every relay-side `BRIDGE_DATA` (`RelayMessage::BridgeData` falls into an empty match arm in `crates/scp-transport/src/native/client.rs` and `adapter.rs`), so a node behind a bridge handles nothing a peer sends it. This story serves each session the bridge opens as one connection of the self-hosted relay's frame handling, multiplexed over its one bridge connection, under the credit, session bound and close rules of §10.12.4, and gives a peer one call that opens a session through a bridge and exchanges ADR-004 frames over it, which the tier 3 KeyPackage fetch and the tier 3 push registrar (PUSH-035) both use. SCP-344 adds the node's KeyPackage admission (§10.7.1 **KeyPackage admission at the node**). The node's `BRIDGE_REGISTER`, which makes a bridge forward anything to a production node, is tracked by the issue in PUSH-033's `blockedByIssues`; this story's tests register the self-hosted relay with the bridge directly. Function and type names are indicators.
acceptanceCriteria: Sessions are served as connections (§10.12.4 **Sessions**): a `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` from the bridge starts a session that goes through the same frame handling a listener connection goes through, with its own subscriptions and its own per-connection limits, and with each limit ADR-004 keys on an address keyed on the session's `source_tag`, so two sessions carrying one tag share one `rate_limit_publish` allowance and two sessions carrying different tags get one each, and two listener connections from two IPv6 addresses in one /64 likewise share one allowance (ADR-004 `ipv6_source_prefix`), and every relay-to-client frame that handling writes goes back as a `BRIDGE_DATA` with the session's ID, in order. A session payload that does not decode as a client frame gets, on that session, the `ERR` `4000` a listener connection gets for it, and the bridge connection and the other sessions stay open.

Operations work unchanged over a session, each in an in-process test with a bridge whose broker role is enabled, a self-hosted relay registered with it, and a peer holding one session: a `PUBLISH` gets `OK` with `blob_id` and the blob is stored; a `QUERY` at a routing ID holding three blobs gets three `BLOB` frames and the `query_complete` `EVENT`; a `SUBSCRIBE` gets its `OK`, its backfill `BLOB` frames and `backfill_complete`, and a blob a listener client publishes at that routing ID afterwards reaches the peer as a live `BLOB` on the session; an `ACK` for that delivery gets the handling and the answer it gets on a listener connection; a `DELETE` gets the answer it gets on a listener connection and an `UNSUBSCRIBE` gets `OK`; a `PING` gets `PONG`; a refused operation gets its `ERR`. Each inner frame echoes the inner `ref` the peer set.

Multiplexing (§10.12.4 **Sessions**): two peers, each holding one session to one self-hosted relay, subscribe to different routing IDs; each live delivery reaches only the session that subscribed, and closing one session ends its subscriptions and leaves the other session's intact. The self-hosted relay sends session frames only on the connection that carries its `BRIDGE_REGISTER` registration and on no listener connection.

Credit at the self-hosted relay (§10.12.4 **Backpressure**): the self-hosted relay grants the bridge at least `max_blob_size` plus 1,024 bytes of credit when it receives the bridge's `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN`, before any other frame for the session, and grants more as it consumes frames, and it sends no `BRIDGE_DATA` beyond the credit the bridge granted it. A test in which the peer grants no credit shows the self-hosted relay's frames for that session wait while its other sessions keep flowing, and the waiting session is closed with `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` `4012` when its held frames would exceed the self-hosted relay's held-frame bound.

Session bound and close (§10.12.4 **Caps**, **Closing**, **Connection loss**): the self-hosted relay's session bound and held-frame bound are named fields of its flat relay config (ADR-052), defaulting to 256 sessions and 1 MiB, held in no global; a `BRIDGE_SESSION_OPEN` beyond the session bound is answered with `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` `4012`. After a `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` from the bridge, after its own `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE`, and after its bridge connection closes, the self-hosted relay holds no state for the session, which a test asserts by the session table's length, the session's subscriptions end, and a later frame naming that session ID produces no frame.

Peer session call: the native relay client exposes one call that opens a session through a bridge to a target routing ID and returns a handle on which the caller sends client frames and receives the self-hosted relay's frames in order, with credit granted and honoured inside the call, including the opening grant of at least `max_blob_size` plus 1,024 bytes when the bridge's `OK` arrives (indicator name: `open_bridge_session`); dropping or closing the handle sends `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` `0`. It returns typed errors that keep apart `4030`, `4031`, `4032` and `4003` on open, a session the bridge or the self-hosted relay closed (carrying the `BRIDGE_SESSION_CLOSE` code), and a dropped connection, and it never surfaces a frame of a session ID it did not open. Unit tests cover each.

KeyPackage read through a bridge (§10.7.1 **Recipient key**, **What bounds the read**): an in-process test stores 2,500 valid KeyPackages of the self-hosted relay's identity at its KeyPackage routing ID (`09-security-model.md` §9.7.4 **KeyPackage routing ID**) and reads all 2,500 on one session with three `QUERY` frames of `limit` 1,000, paged with `since` and `after_blob`, the `query_complete` counts being 1,000, 1,000 and 500 and each `BLOB` byte-for-byte equal to the stored blob; with the bridge's rate cap lowered under a paused Tokio clock, the same read completes after the clock advances and the session is never closed.

The KeyPackage publisher cites the definition of the routing ID it publishes at (`09-security-model.md` §9.7.4 **KeyPackage routing ID**): the `ContextTransportProvider` publish method doc in `crates/scp-runtime/src/context/builder.rs` and the publish comment in `crates/scp-transport/src/provider.rs`, which cite `spec §5.12.3` for `derive_key_package_routing_id` today, cite `09-security-model.md` §9.7.4 instead. A unit test in `crates/scp-transport/src/provider.rs` computes `SHA-256(BE32(len(did)) || did || "scp-key-packages")` with `sha2` directly for one fixture identifier and asserts that the routing ID the provider publishes a KeyPackage at equals those 32 bytes. The Welcome-delivery citation of §5.12.3 in `builder.rs` is correct and stays. Check: `git grep -n -A1 derive_key_package_routing_id -- crates/scp-runtime/src/context/builder.rs crates/scp-transport/src/provider.rs` prints no line containing `§5.12.3`.
actionItems: Serve each bridge session from the self-hosted relay's bridge connection as one connection of the relay's frame handling, with a per-session sink and credit.
Add the peer-side session call to the native relay client.
Add the in-process bridge tests.

stories.title: A relay deletes a blob only for a DELETE that presents the token whose hash a PUBLISH of that blob carried
stories.description: Implements ADR-004 operations 1 and 5 as amended 2026-10-20 and `10-infrastructure-and-self-hosting.md` §10.4 **Deletion is bound to the publisher** and §10.7.1 **No DELETE at that routing ID**. Today four relay handlers answer `DELETE`: `handle_delete` in `crates/scp-transport/src/native/server.rs`, `handle_delete` in `crates/scp-transport/src/quic/listener.rs` (which a node starts in `crates/scp-node/src/http.rs`), `handle_udp_delete` in `crates/scp-transport/src/udp/listener.rs`, and `handle_delete_inner` in `crates/scp-transport/src/webtransport/session.rs`. Each runs `DidSlotRegistry::gate_delete` (`did_slot.rs`), which rejects only a protected DID-record slot, and then calls `storage.delete`, so any party that sends a `QUERY` at a routing ID can delete every blob stored there: the KeyPackages a tier 3 client reads, pending Commits and Welcomes, and broadcast chunks. A PUBLISH now carries `delete_token_hash = SHA-256("scp-relay-delete-v1:" || blob_id || delete_token)` (`09-security-model.md` §9.18.2), the relay keeps each hash as a delete claim on the blob, and a `DELETE` presents the token. No SDK or FFI bridge exposes a relay blob delete today (`git grep -n -i delete -- bindings crates/scp-ffi` finds storage and context deletes only), so no binding changes; the adapters that send ADR-004's `DELETE` are listed by `git grep -n 'fn delete(&self, blob_id: &BlobId)' -- crates/scp-transport/src`. File locations and type names are indicators.
acceptanceCriteria: Wire (ADR-004 client table): `ClientMessage::Publish` carries `delete_token_hash: Option<[u8; 32]>` and `ClientMessage::Delete` carries `delete_token: [u8; 32]` (indicator: `crates/scp-relay-client/src/protocol.rs`), under the field names the table gives, and the QUIC binding's `DELETE` frame (`crates/scp-transport/src/quic/streams.rs`) carries the same field. `crates/scp-relay-client/src/error.rs` defines `4043` DELETE_UNAUTHORIZED and the constant-value test asserts it. Round-trip tests encode and decode both frames, and a `DELETE` frame without `delete_token` is answered with `4002` MISSING_FIELD.

One deletion path: every relay handler that answers `DELETE` (indicators: the four handlers named above) decides and performs the deletion through one function shared at the level of `DidSlotRegistry::gate_delete`, which runs the rate gate, the retained-kind check, the node KeyPackage routing ID refusal and the claim check, and deletes the blob only when the last claim is presented; no handler calls `storage.delete` for a `DELETE` itself (shown by `git grep -n 'storage.delete\|storage.as_ref().delete' -- crates/scp-transport/src/native/server.rs crates/scp-transport/src/quic/listener.rs crates/scp-transport/src/udp/listener.rs crates/scp-transport/src/webtransport/session.rs` finding no `DELETE` handler). The claim, copy, retained-kind and node routing ID cases below run against each of the four listeners (WebSocket, QUIC, UDP/DTLS, WebTransport), each driven through its own wire handler rather than the shared function alone.

Claims (ADR-004 operation 5): in an in-process relay test, a blob published with the hash of token t1 is deleted by a `DELETE` carrying t1, which gets `OK`, after which a `QUERY` returns nothing; the same blob published again survives a `DELETE` carrying any other 32 bytes, which gets `4043`; a `DELETE` of a `blob_id` the relay never stored gets `4043`; and a blob published without `delete_token_hash` survives every `DELETE`, each answered `4043`, until its TTL. A test computes `SHA-256("scp-relay-delete-v1:" || blob_id || t1)` with `sha2` directly and asserts that the relay's stored claim equals those 32 bytes.

Copies: a second PUBLISH of the same blob with the hash of t2 adds a claim, so a `DELETE` carrying t2 gets `OK` and a `QUERY` still returns the blob, and a `DELETE` carrying t1 then gets `OK` and the blob is gone. A blob holding 16 claims answers a 17th PUBLISH with `OK` and adds no claim, shown by a `DELETE` carrying the 17th token getting `4043`. Claims survive a restart of each persistent backend (SQLite, redb, Postgres, S3), shown by claim cases added to the `blob_store_conformance!()` suite that every backend runs.

Retained kinds and the node's KeyPackage routing ID: a `DELETE` of a blob at a retained kind still gets `4041` whatever token it carries, and a `retain` write that carries `delete_token_hash` stores no claim. A node's relay, which receives its identity's KeyPackage routing ID through its flat relay config (ADR-052), answers `4043` to a `DELETE` of a blob at that routing ID that carries the blob's own token, and a `QUERY` still returns the blob; the same `DELETE` of a blob at another routing ID deletes it. The rate gate of `DidSlotRegistry::gate_delete` still runs before the token check.

Client adapters: the native relay adapter's `send` draws a fresh 32-byte token from a CSPRNG for every PUBLISH, sends its hash as `delete_token_hash`, and keeps the token by `blob_id` until the blob's TTL ends in a token store defined as a trait before its implementations (indicator name: `DeleteTokenStore`), which the adapter's construction receives through its initializer (ADR-052), whose production implementation persists in the instance's storage, and which no global, singleton or `static` holds. `delete(blob_id)` sends a `DELETE` with that token, and returns a typed error and sends nothing for a `blob_id` it holds no token for. A test with two recording relays shows one blob sent to both carries two different hashes. Every other adapter that sends ADR-004's `DELETE` (indicators: `quic/adapter.rs`, `udp/adapter.rs`, `webtransport/client.rs`, `coap/adapter.rs`) does the same, each with a test.
actionItems: Add `delete_token_hash` and `delete_token` to the wire types and `4043` to the codes.
Store delete claims with each blob in every backend, and route every relay `DELETE` handler (WebSocket, QUIC, UDP/DTLS, WebTransport) through one shared claim-checking deletion function.
Draw, keep and present tokens in each adapter that sends `DELETE`.

stories.title: A node's relay admits at its identity's KeyPackage routing ID only KeyPackages that verify for the identity under a device's Current wrapping key, and retires consumed init keys
stories.description: Implements `10-infrastructure-and-self-hosting.md` §10.7.1 **KeyPackage admission at the node**, **Low-s**, **What the publisher counts**, **Retired init keys** and **A republished old key**, at the node's relay that SCP-340 serves on bridge sessions. The admission was part of SCP-340 and moved here so that bridge sessions can start before its wrapping-key condition can be checked: that condition reads the per-device wrapping-key role that keri P7 adds to the identity's key state (`09-security-model.md` §9.7.4.2), which has no story ID yet, and the issue in `blockedByIssues` tracks it. Function and type names are indicators.
acceptanceCriteria: KeyPackage admission at the node (§10.7.1 **KeyPackage admission at the node**, ADR-004 `4042`): `crates/scp-relay-client/src/error.rs` defines `4042` KEY_PACKAGE_REJECTED and the constant-value test asserts it. In an in-process test, a PUBLISH at the node identity's KeyPackage routing ID is refused with `ERR` `4042` and stores nothing in each of these cases, sent both on a listener connection and on a bridge session: a blob that does not decode as a KeyPackage; a valid KeyPackage followed by one padding byte; the ECDSA twin `(r, n − s)` of a valid KeyPackage's signature, which verifies but is high-s; a KeyPackage whose attestation names a wrapping key the identity's key state lists `Current` for no device, once for a key it lists `Superseded` and once for a key in no entry; a valid KeyPackage whose bytes differ from its own re-serialization, made by rewriting one vector length header in more bytes than it needs; a KeyPackage whose own signature under its `leaf_node.signature_key` fails (RFC 9420 §10.1), made by changing one byte of its extensions or capabilities after signing; a KeyPackage with no `scp_keypackage_attestation`; one whose attestation names another identifier; one signed by a key the identity's key state does not list `Current` in the `#active` role; one whose `expires_at` is at or before the node's clock; and one whose `issued_at` is more than 300 seconds after the node's clock. A valid KeyPackage of the identity is stored and answered with `OK` and `blob_id`. One copy per `init_key`: a second PUBLISH of a stored valid KeyPackage gets `OK` with the stored `blob_id`, and a query then returns exactly one blob for that `init_key`. Valid KeyPackages of two devices, each naming its own device's `Current` wrapping key, are both stored. After one device's wrapping-key entry stops being `Current`, a query returns no KeyPackage naming that key and still returns the other device's. A PUBLISH of the same junk blob at any other routing ID is stored as before. A query after the refusals returns only the stored valid KeyPackages. The device's publish path counts a KeyPackage the node answered with `4042` as not published: a test in which the node refuses one of ten published KeyPackages finds the device's count of published unused KeyPackages is nine (`09-security-model.md` §9.7.4).

Low-s minting and retired init keys (§10.7.1 **Low-s**, **Retired init keys**, `03-identity.md` §3.7.1.1 `RetireInitKey`): every KeyPackage the KeyPackage minting and publish path produces carries an ECDSA signature whose `s` is at most n/2 (indicators: `generate_key_package` in `crates/scp-mls/src/group.rs`, `publish_key_package` in `crates/scp-transport/src/provider.rs`); a test mints 1,000 KeyPackages and checks every signature, and a test hands the publish path a KeyPackage re-signed into high-s form and finds it refuses to publish it with a typed error. In-process tests with the node's instance and a second device of the identity sharing its private state: after the second device consumes an `init_key` at a join, it appends a `RetireInitKey` event, and once the node's instance reads it a query no longer returns that KeyPackage and a PUBLISH of it gets `ERR` `4042` and stores nothing; the same holds after the node's own instance consumes one, and after either device deletes one; under a test clock, a retired entry is gone once its `expires_at` passes, and the set survives a restart of the node's instance. The retired-init-key set is a field of a type the node's construction receives through its initializer (ADR-052), and no global, singleton or `static` holds it.
actionItems: Add the admission check at the node identity's KeyPackage routing ID, on listener connections and bridge sessions.
Mint KeyPackages in low-s form and refuse to publish a high-s one.
Append `RetireInitKey` on consume and delete, and keep the node's retired-init-key set.
